citations.quote:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Let $V,W$ be nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner product spaces with orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_m)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_n)$ of $W$, let $V\otimes W$ be their tensor product with the inner product of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], and let $\operatorname{tr}$ denote the basis-independent trace of an endomorphism ([[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]).

(a) For every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$ there is a unique endomorphism $\operatorname{Tr}_W R$ of $V$ with

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_WR)A\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R(A\otimes I_W)\bigr)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\operatorname{End}(V),$$

namely $\operatorname{Tr}_WR=\sum_{j=1}^n\varphi_j\circ R\circ\iota_j$, where $\iota_j(v)=v\otimes f_j$ and $\varphi_j(x\otimes w)=\langle w,f_j\rangle x$; it does not depend on the orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $W$, and the analogous definition gives $\operatorname{Tr}_V R$ with $\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_VR)B)=\operatorname{tr}(R(I_V\otimes B))$.

(b) $\operatorname{Tr}_W$ is linear, positive (it maps positive endomorphisms to positive endomorphisms) and trace preserving on density matrices: if $R\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}R=1$ then $\operatorname{Tr}_WR\ge0$ and $\operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Tr}_WR=1$; and $\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}=CC^*$ for every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$, where $C:W\to V$ is the coefficient map determined by $\Psi=\sum_jCf_j\otimes f_j$.

(c) *Schmidt decomposition.* Every $\Psi\in V\otimes W$ admits an expansion

$$\Psi=\sum_{r=1}^{k}s_r\,v_r\otimes u_r,$$

with $k\le\min(m,n)$, orthonormal families $(v_r)\subseteq V$, $(u_r)\subseteq W$ and $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_k>0$ uniquely determined by $\Psi$ as the positive singular values of the coefficient map; moreover $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_rs_r^2$. For $\|\Psi\|=1$ the reduced density $\rho=\operatorname{Tr}_W T_{\Psi,\Psi}$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=\sum_rs_r^4$, and $\operatorname{tr}\rho^2=1$ holds exactly when $k=1$, i.e. exactly when $\Psi$ is a product vector; mixed-state separability is not decided by this criterion.

(d) *Finite nonselective no-signalling.* If $(M_a)_{a=1}^p$ are endomorphisms of $W$ with $\sum_aM_a^*M_a=I_W$ then for every endomorphism $R$ of $V\otimes W$

$$\operatorname{Tr}_W\Bigl(\sum_a(I_V\otimes M_a)R(I_V\otimes M_a^*)\Bigr)=\operatorname{Tr}_WR .$$

This is an identity for the specified finite local instrument; selective conditioning (dividing one summand by its nonzero trace) is not covered.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). Recall that $T_{u,v}\in\mathcal B(H)$ denotes the rank-one operator $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]).

(a) A **density operator** on $H$ is a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). If $(u_n)_{n\in J}$ is a finite or countable orthonormal family, with $J$ a finite initial segment of the positive integers or all positive integers, and $w_n\ge0$ with $\sum_nw_n=1$, then the sum $\rho:=\sum_nw_nT_{u_n,u_n}$ converges in trace norm to a density operator with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$. Conversely every density operator $\rho$ admits such an expansion whose weights are its positive eigenvalues counted with multiplicity and whose vectors are orthonormal eigenvectors; distinct expansions of the same $\rho$ exist when a positive eigenspace has dimension at least two.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

(c) Assume in addition the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with projection-valued measure $E_A$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let $\psi\in H$ have $\|\psi\|=1$ and $\psi\in D(A)$. Here $|A|^{1/2}$ denotes the unbounded PVM integral $f(E_A)$ for $f(\lambda)=|\lambda|^{1/2}$, with domain $D(f(E_A))=\{\psi:\int |\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}<\infty\}$ as in [[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]. Then

$$\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle,\qquad \int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)=\|A\psi\|^2 ,$$

where $E_{A,\psi}(B)=\langle E_A(B)\psi,\psi\rangle$ ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]); moreover $\int_{\mathbb R}|\lambda|\,dE_{A,\psi}(\lambda)<\infty$ exactly when $\psi\in D(|A|^{1/2})$, and then the mean $\int\lambda\,dE_{A,\psi}$ is finite. No product $A\rho$ of an unbounded operator with a density operator is used, and no physical interpretation of $\mu_\rho$ or of the moments is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ and
$K$ be Hilbert spaces over the same field $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$
([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a compact operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]])
with zero-padded singular-value sequence $(s_n(T))_{n\ge1}$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]).

**Trace class.** The operator $T$ is **trace class** when
$$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)<+\infty .$$
Thus the series in the zero-based convention of
[[def-series-and-absolute-convergence-in-a-normed-space]] is formed from the
explicit sequence $(s_{m+1}(T))_{m\in\mathbb N}$. In that case its **trace
norm** is
$$\|T\|_1:=\sum_{m\in\mathbb N}s_{m+1}(T)\in[0,+\infty),$$
and $\|T\|_1$ is also written $\|T\|_{\mathrm{tr}}$. The set of trace-class
operators $H\to K$ is written $\mathcal S_1(H,K)$.

**Immediate consequences.** Since $0\le s_n(T)\le s_1(T)=\|T\|$
([[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]), the terms
are nonnegative and $\|T\|_1\ge\|T\|\ge0$ whenever $T$ is trace class; the zero
operator is trace class with $\|0\|_1=0$. When $T$ has finite rank $r$ the
sequence is zero-padded, the series is the finite sum
$\sum_{n=1}^r s_n(T)=\sum_{\lambda>0}\lambda\dim_{\mathbb F} E_\lambda(|T|)$ over the finitely
many positive eigenvalues of $|T|$ counted with multiplicity ([[def-dimension]]),
and every finite-rank operator is compact
([[lem-finite-rank-operators-are-compact]]) and therefore trace class; in particular every
operator with finite-dimensional range and every rank-one operator is trace
class. If $T$ has infinite rank then $s_n(T)>0$ for every $n$ and the series
$\sum_{n\ge1}s_n(T)$ converges in the summable case. By the necessary
condition for convergence of a scalar series ([[lem-nth-term-test]]), a
trace-class operator with infinite rank has $s_n(T)\to0$, hence
is a norm limit of finite-rank operators
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]]).

**Choice accounting.** Trace class is defined through the singular values of
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]], whose
construction uses $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ through the countable selection of finite
orthonormal bases of the eigenspaces of $|T|$ and the spectral theorem; no
Hilbert basis of the ambient space, and no stronger choice, is used here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$
be a trace-class operator on $H$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let $E$ be a
Hilbert basis of $H$, **supplied as data**
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]];
existence of such a basis is not asserted here). The **trace of $T$ relative to
$E$** is
$$\operatorname{tr}_E(T):=\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle,$$
the sum of the scalar family $(\langle Te,e\rangle)_{e\in E}$ in the
finite-subset-net sense of
[[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]].

**The family is absolutely summable, uniformly in $E$.** Let
$T=\sum_js_j\langle\cdot,e_j\rangle f_j$ be the singular-value series
([[thm-singular-value-decomposition-for-compact-operators]],
[[def-absolute-value-and-singular-values-of-a-compact-operator]]) with
$(e_j)_{j\in J}$, $(f_j)_{j\in J}$ orthonormal and $\sum_js_j=\|T\|_1<+\infty$
([[def-trace-class-operator]]). For every $e\in H$ the series
$\langle Te,e\rangle=\sum_{j}s_j\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle$
converges absolutely, because the moduli are bounded by
$s_1\sum_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le s_1\|e\|^2$ by
Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]],
[[lem-finite-bessel-inequality]]). Consequently, for every finite
$F\subseteq E$, using the interchange of finite sums with the nonnegative
finite-subset supremum over $j$ and then finite Cauchy–Schwarz and Bessel twice,
$$\sum_{e\in F}|\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\sum_{e\in F}\sum_{j}s_j|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|=\sum_{j}s_j\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|\,|\langle f_j,e\rangle|\le\sum_{j}s_j\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle e,e_j\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{e\in F}|\langle f_j,e\rangle|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le\sum_{j}s_j=\|T\|_1 ,$$
because for each $j$ the two finite coefficient sums are bounded by
$\|e_j\|=1$ and $\|f_j\|=1$ (finite Bessel). Hence the finite subsums of
$|(\langle Te,e\rangle)|_{e\in E}$ are bounded by $\|T\|_1$, the family is
absolutely summable, and an absolutely summable family of scalars is summable in
ZF with $|\sum_{e\in E}\langle Te,e\rangle|\le\|T\|_1$
([[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]). This justifies the
notation $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ before any basis-independence statement.

**Choice accounting and status.** Only a supplied basis $E$ and the singular
values of $T$ are used; no Hilbert basis of $H$ is assumed to exist, and the
next theorem proves that $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)$ does not depend on the
supplied basis and equals the basis-free trace of $T$
([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]).

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $X$ be a normed space, let $D \subseteq X$ be a dense normed subspace, let
$Y$ be a Banach space, and let $T:D\to Y$ be a bounded linear operator. Then
there is a unique bounded linear operator $\widetilde T:X\to Y$ such that

$$\widetilde T|_D = T,$$

and $\|\widetilde T\| = \|T\|$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

derivations.claim: [The parenthesisation isometry] For $n=1$, $J_1u=u\otimes1$ is an isometry by [F1], and every tensor in $H\widehat\otimes\mathbb C$ equals $u\otimes1$, so it is surjective. For $n\ge2$, the map $(v_1,\dots,v_n)\mapsto v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$ is multilinear from $H^n$ into $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$, so by [F2] applied to the two parenthesisations of the $n$-fold algebraic tensor product it defines a linear map on the algebraic tensor product, and this linear map preserves inner products on elementary tensors by [F1]: $\langle v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle=\prod_k\langle v_k,w_k\rangle=\langle v_1,w_1\rangle\langle v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n,w_2\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n\rangle$. Since the elementary tensors span a dense subspace and both sides are complete, [F8] and this isometry identity give a linear isometry $J_n$ on the completed tensor powers, and the image is closed and contains all elementary tensors $v_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)$, whose span is dense by [F1]; hence $J_n$ is surjective. This proves (b).

[The first-slot operator] By [F3] the operator $O\otimes I_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}\in\mathcal B(H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)})$ is bounded with $(O\otimes I)(u\otimes w)=Ou\otimes w$. Transporting it through the isometry $J_n$ of clause (b) gives a bounded operator $A_1:=J_n^{-1}(O\otimes I)J_n$ on $H^{\otimes n}$ with $A_1(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=J_n^{-1}(Ov_1\otimes(v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n))=Ov_1\otimes v_2\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$ for all $v_1,\dots,v_n\in H$.

[The zero extension and its symmetry] With $j$ the inclusion of the sector, $\widetilde\rho=j\rho j^*$ restricts to $\rho$ on the sector and vanishes on its orthogonal complement. It is self-adjoint and positive because $\langle\widetilde\rho x,x\rangle=\langle\rho j^*x,j^*x\rangle\ge0$; adjoining an orthonormal basis of the complement to one of the sector gives $\operatorname{tr}\widetilde\rho=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$, so it is a density operator by [F6]. Since $jj^*=P_\sigma^{(n)}$ and $U_\pi j=\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)j$ by [F4], $\widetilde\rho=P_\sigma^{(n)}\widetilde\rho P_\sigma^{(n)}$ and $U_\pi\widetilde\rho U_\pi^*=\widetilde\rho$ for every $\pi$. A zero sector admits no trace-one endomorphism, so no $\rho$ exists in that case.

[Slot operators and the permutation invariance of their sum] Fix $i$, choose $\pi\in S_n$ with $\widehat{\pi}(1)=i$ and set $O^{(i)}:=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$; [F9] and step 1.2 give $\|O^{(i)}\|=\|O\otimes I\|\le\|O\|$, and [F3], [F4] give $(O^{(i)})^*=U_\pi J_n^{-1}(O^*\otimes I)J_nU_\pi^*=(O^*)^{(i)}$, so $O=O^*$ gives $O^{(i)}=(O^{(i)})^*$. On elementary tensors, [F4] gives $U_\pi^*(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_{\widehat{\pi}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\widehat{\pi}(n)}$; step 1.2 replaces the first factor by $Ov_{\widehat{\pi}(1)}=Ov_i$; and $U_\pi$ then moves that factor to slot $\widehat{\pi}(1)=i$, leaving every other factor in its original slot, so $O^{(i)}(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes Ov_i\otimes\cdots\otimes v_n$. If $\pi'$ is another permutation with $\widehat{\pi'}(1)=i$, then $\tau:=\pi^{-1}\pi'$ has $\widehat{\tau}(1)=1$ and $U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*$ agrees with $A_1$ on elementary tensors by [F1], [F3], hence equals it by [F8]; thus $U_{\pi'}A_1U_{\pi'}^*=U_\pi U_\tau A_1U_\tau^*U_\pi^*=U_\pi A_1U_\pi^*$ and $O^{(i)}$ is well defined, with the displayed elementary-tensor action. For $\tau\in S_n$ one then has $U_\tau O^{(i)}U_\tau^*=U_{\tau\pi}A_1U_{\tau\pi}^*=O^{(\widehat{\tau}(i))}$, and summing over $i$ with $\widehat{\tau}$ permuting $\{1,\dots,n\}$ gives $U_\tau\Sigma(O)U_\tau^*=\Sigma(O)$ for $\Sigma(O):=\sum_{i=1}^nO^{(i)}$; equivalently $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with every $U_\tau$. Since $P_\sigma^{(n)}=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}_\sigma(\pi)U_\pi$ is a finite linear combination of the $U_\pi$ by [F4], $\Sigma(O)$ commutes with $P_\sigma^{(n)}$, so it preserves $\mathfrak H_n^\sigma$ and its orthogonal complement and $\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)=P_\sigma^{(n)}\Sigma(O)P_\sigma^{(n)}$; this proves (a) and (c).

[Reduction to one slot, the trace law and the reduced operator] By steps 1.3 and 2.1 and [F7], for $\widehat{\pi}(1)=i$ one has $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho O^{(i)})=\operatorname{tr}(U_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi A_1)=\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)$. Set $R_n:=J_n\widetilde\rho J_n^{-1}$, an endomorphism of $H\widehat\otimes H^{\otimes(n-1)}$. Its partial trace $\gamma:=\operatorname{Tr}_{H^{\otimes(n-1)}}R_n$ is an endomorphism of $H$ by [F5]. Step 1.2 and [F5], [F7] give $\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\Sigma(O))=n\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho A_1)=n\operatorname{tr}(R_n(O\otimes I))=n\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)$, proving (d). Unitary transport by $J_n$ preserves positivity and trace, so $R_n$ is positive of trace one; [F5] then makes $\gamma$ positive of trace one and hence a density operator on $H$ by [F6]. For the retained slot $i$, use $J_nU_\pi^*$ as the parenthesisation map; its transported state is $J_nU_\pi^*\widetilde\rho U_\pi J_n^{-1}=R_n$ by step 1.3, so its partial trace is the same $\gamma$. More generally the pairing $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma O)=n^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\widetilde\rho\Sigma(O))$ for every $O$ uniquely determines $\gamma$: testing against $O=T_{u,v}$ gives $\operatorname{tr}(\gamma T_{u,v})=\langle\gamma u,v\rangle$ by [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] clause (e), which determines every matrix entry. For $n=1$, $J_1u=u\otimes1$, $P_\sigma^{(1)}=I$ and $\Sigma(O)=O$, so this pairing gives $\gamma=\rho$. This proves (e), including the one-particle boundary.

[Conclusion and scope] Step 1.1 proves (b), step 2.1 proves (a) and (c), and step 3.1 proves (d) and (e); every argument used only the finite-dimensional tensor construction, the permutation sectors, the partial trace and the trace axioms, and no physical object, preparation or measurement entered, which is clause (f).

boundaries.evidence: Owning focused62 proof/interface review confirmed. Zero sector has no trace-one density operator, so clauses(d)-(e) have no preparation instance; labelled slot identities still hold. Anchors: Statement and step 1.3.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$\mathfrak H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension
$d\ge1$ with inner product linear in the first argument
([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $H:\mathfrak H\to\mathfrak H$ be a self-adjoint
linear operator with real eigenvalues $E_1,\dots,E_d$ (repeated according to
multiplicity) and orthonormal eigenbasis $(v_1,\dots,v_d)$, and let $\beta>0$.
Write
$$Z:=\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-\beta E_j}\in(0,\infty),\qquad \rho_\beta:=\frac1Z\sum_{j=1}^d e^{-\beta E_j}T_{v_j,v_j},$$
where $T_{u,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle u$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). Let
$\mathcal D$ be the set of density operators on $\mathfrak H$, i.e. positive
self-adjoint trace-class operators $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$
([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]), and
for $\rho\in\mathcal D$ with eigenvalues $w_1,\dots,w_d\ge0$ (counted with
multiplicity and in any order) define the entropy
$$s(\rho):=-\sum_{i:\,w_i>0}w_i\log w_i\in[0,\log d]$$
([[def-natural-logarithm]]). Then:

(a) $\rho_\beta\in\mathcal D$, $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\frac1Z\sum_je^{-\beta E_j}E_j$,
and
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=-\beta^{-1}\log Z ;$$

(b) for every $\rho\in\mathcal D$,
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho)\ \ge\ -\beta^{-1}\log Z ;$$

(c) for every $\rho\in\mathcal D$, $s(\rho)\le\log d$, with $s(\rho)=\log d$ if
and only if $\rho=d^{-1}\,\mathrm{id}$; when $H=0$ one has $Z=d$,
$\rho_\beta=d^{-1}\mathrm{id}$ and the bound in (b) is attained there.

The combination $\operatorname{tr}(\rho H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho)$ is a purely
mathematical functional of $(\rho,H,\beta)$; identifying $\beta$ with an
inverse physical temperature and $\rho_\beta$ with a thermal equilibrium state
are additional physical assumptions not asserted here.

For every natural $n$, the map
$\operatorname{tr}:M_n(F)\to F$ is linear:

$$\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)+\operatorname{tr}(B),\qquad \operatorname{tr}(\lambda A)=\lambda\operatorname{tr}(A).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]) and let
$S\in\mathcal B(H)$ be bounded. Then $ST$ and $TS$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(ST)=\operatorname{tr}(TS) .$$
If $A,B\in\mathcal B(H)$ are Hilbert–Schmidt relative to a supplied Hilbert
basis $E$ of $H$ ([[def-hilbert-schmidt-operator]]), then the products $AB$ and
$BA$ are trace class and
$$\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: [Exponential comparison] Since $\beta\varepsilon>0$, strict increase in [F3] gives $\exp(\beta\varepsilon)>\exp(0)=1$, and [F3] gives $\exp(-\beta\varepsilon)=1/\exp(\beta\varepsilon)\in(0,1)$; consequently $1<Z=1+\exp(-\beta\varepsilon)<2$.

[The canonical operator] By [F1] with $E_0=0$, $E_1=\varepsilon$ and $(v_1,v_2)=(u_0,u_1)$, $Z=1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}$ and $\rho_\beta=Z^{-1}(T_{u_0,u_0}+e^{-\beta\varepsilon}T_{u_1,u_1})\in\mathcal D$, so $\rho_\beta$ is a density operator; its two weights are $Z^{-1}$ and $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}Z^{-1}$, which are distinct because $\exp(-\beta\varepsilon)\ne1$ by step 1.1.

[Mean energy, entropy and free energy] Using [F2] and $T_{u_0,u_0}T_{u_1,u_1}=\langle u_1,u_0\rangle T_{u_0,u_1}=0$ by orthogonality, and $T_{u_1,u_1}T_{u_1,u_1}=T_{u_1,u_1}$ with $\langle u_1,u_1\rangle=1$, the product $\rho_\beta H$ equals $\varepsilon e^{-\beta\varepsilon}Z^{-1}T_{u_1,u_1}$, so [F2] gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\varepsilon e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/Z$; by step 1.1, $e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/Z=e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})=1/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)$, hence $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\varepsilon/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)$ lies in $(0,\varepsilon/2)$. By [F1], $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=-\beta^{-1}\log Z$, so $s(\rho_\beta)=\log Z+\beta\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)=\log(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})+\beta\varepsilon/(e^{\beta\varepsilon}+1)=\log(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})+\beta\varepsilon e^{-\beta\varepsilon}/(1+e^{-\beta\varepsilon})$; by [F1] and [F2], $0\le s(\rho_\beta)<\log2$ because $\rho_\beta\ne\tfrac12\mathrm{id}$ by step 2.1. Finally $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_\beta H)-\beta^{-1}s(\rho_\beta)=-\beta^{-1}\log Z=F$ with $F$ as defined. This proves (b) and (c), and step 2.1 proved (a).

[Conclusion] Steps 1.1-2.1 prove (a), step 3.1 proves (b) and (c), and every identity is an algebraic consequence of the supplied finite-dimensional formulas and the real exponential and logarithm laws, which is (d).

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H,H',K,K'$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $S\in\mathcal B(H,H')$, $T\in\mathcal B(K,K')$ be bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Write $H\widehat\otimes K$ for the completion of the algebraic tensor product constructed in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], with inclusion $\kappa$.

(a) There is a unique bounded linear operator $S\otimes T: H\widehat\otimes K\to H'\widehat\otimes K'$ with $(S\otimes T)\kappa(u\otimes v)=\kappa'(Su\otimes Tv)$ for all $u\in H$, $v\in K$, and it satisfies $\|S\otimes T\|\le\|S\|\,\|T\|$ ([[def-operator-norm]]).

(b) For Hilbert spaces $H'',K''$ and bounded $S':H''\to H$, $T':K''\to K$, one has $(S\otimes T)(S'\otimes T')=(SS')\otimes(TT')$. In particular, for endomorphisms $S:H\to H$, $T:K\to K$, the endomorphisms $S\otimes I_K$ and $I_H\otimes T$ commute and their composite is $S\otimes T$.

(c) The Hilbert adjoint ([[def-hilbert-space-adjoint]]) is $(S\otimes T)^*=S^*\otimes T^*$.

(d) If $S,T$ are unitary, then so is $S\otimes T$. No extension of unbounded maps, and no algebraic manipulation of domains of unbounded operators, is asserted.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

**Slot convention.** For $\ell\ge1$, $S_\ell$ acts on $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. On one-based tuple positions use $\widehat{\pi}(k):=1+\pi(k-1)$ for $1\le k\le\ell$. Conjugation by $k\mapsto k-1$ gives $\widehat{\pi\sigma}=\widehat{\pi}\circ\widehat{\sigma}$ and $\widehat{\pi^{-1}}=\widehat{\pi}^{-1}$; thus the supplier's tensor action becomes $U_\pi(v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_\ell)=v_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\widehat{\pi}^{-1}(\ell)}$. The parameters of $U_\pi$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ remain canonical zero-based permutations.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$ with orthonormal basis
$(e_1,\dots,e_d)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Let
$n\ge1$, and let $H^{\otimes n}$ be the $n$-fold completed tensor power with
$H^{\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$, $H^{\otimes1}:=H$ and
$H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$
([[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]), and let
$P_\pm^{(n)}\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$, $n\ge1$, be the permutation
projections of [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. For a
multi-index $i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n$ write
$$e_i:=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_n},\qquad |i|_j:=\#\{k:i_k=j\}\ (j=1,\dots,d).$$
For $J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}$ with $|J|=n$, written $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_n\}$, put
$$e_J^\wedge:=\frac1{\sqrt{n!}}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\, e_{j_{\widehat{\sigma}(1)}}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_{\widehat{\sigma}(n)}},$$
and for $\lambda\in W(n,d):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb N^d:\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ put
$\operatorname{orb}(\lambda):=\{c\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n:|c|=\lambda\}$ and
$m_\lambda:=\sum_{c\in\operatorname{orb}(\lambda)}e_c$. Then:

(a) *product basis*: $(e_i)_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}$ is an orthonormal basis of
$H^{\otimes n}$, and $\dim H^{\otimes n}=d^n$;

(b) *Slater basis*: for every $J$ with $|J|=n$ one has
$e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ and the
family $(e_J^\wedge)_{J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\},\ |J|=n}$ is an orthonormal family whose
closed linear span is $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$; it is therefore an
orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$,
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$, and
$\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$ when $n>d$. Moreover for every multi-index
$i$ one has $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ when two entries of $i$ coincide, and
$$P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\,\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$$
when the entries of $i$ are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J$ and
$\rho_i\in S_n$ is the unique permutation with $i_k=j_{\widehat{\rho_i}(k)}$;

(c) *symmetric basis*: for every $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ the vector $m_\lambda$ is
nonzero, the family $(m_\lambda)_{\lambda\in W(n,d)}$ is orthogonal,
$U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$ for every $\pi\in S_n$, and for every multi-index
$i$ there is a real number $\gamma_i>0$ with
$P_+^{(n)}(e_i)=\gamma_i\,m_{|i|}$; consequently
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is the linear span of $(m_\lambda)$, the family
$(m_\lambda)$ is an orthogonal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$;

(d) *occupation operators*: for $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the map
$$N_j:H^{\otimes n}\to H^{\otimes n},\qquad N_jx:=\sum_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}|i|_j\,\langle x,e_i\rangle\,e_i,$$
is a self-adjoint bounded endomorphism, the $N_j$ commute pairwise,
$\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$, and
$$N_je_J^\wedge=\mathbf 1_J(j)\,e_J^\wedge,\qquad N_jm_\lambda=\lambda_j\,m_\lambda .$$
Consequently both sectors are invariant under every $N_j$, the joint
eigenspaces of $(N_1,\dots,N_d)$ inside $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ are the
lines $\mathbb Ce_J^\wedge$ (one for each $n$-element subset $J$, with
eigenvalue vector $\mathbf 1_J$), and the joint eigenspaces inside
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ are the lines $\mathbb Cm_\lambda$ (one for each
$\lambda\in W(n,d)$, with eigenvalue vector $\lambda$).

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, $n\ge1$, and $H^{\otimes n}$ the $n$-fold completed tensor power ($H^{\otimes1}:=H$, $H^{\otimes(k+1)}:=H^{\otimes k}\widehat\otimes H$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]). For $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}\in H$ write $v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1}\in H^{\otimes n}$ for the iterated elementary tensor.

(a) For every $\pi$ in the symmetric group $S_n$ ([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]) there is a unique unitary $U_\pi\in\mathcal B(H^{\otimes n})$ with

$$U_\pi(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=v_{\pi^{-1}(0)}\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{\pi^{-1}(n-1)},$$

and $U_\pi U_\sigma=U_{\pi\sigma}$, $U_{\pi}^*=U_{\pi^{-1}}$.

(b) The operators

$$P_+:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi,\qquad P_-:=\frac1{n!}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$$

(with $\operatorname{sgn}$ the sign homomorphism, [[thm-sign-is-a-homomorphism]]) are orthogonal projections.

(c) $U_\pi P_+=P_+U_\pi=P_+$ and $U_\pi P_-=P_-U_\pi=\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)P_-$ for every $\pi$; consequently the range of $P_+$ is the subspace of vectors fixed by every $U_\pi$, and the range of $P_-$ is the subspace of vectors transforming by $\operatorname{sgn}$.

(d) If $v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}$ have a repeated factor, that is, $v_i=v_j$ for some distinct $i,j\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, then $P_-(v_0\otimes\cdots\otimes v_{n-1})=0$.

Selecting the symmetric or antisymmetric sector for a particle species is a physical postulate, not a theorem of this construction; no spin-statistics statement is proved here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$ with orthonormal basis
$(e_1,\dots,e_d)$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $H^{\otimes n}$ and
$P_\pm^{(n)}$ be as in
[[thm-nrqm-identical-particles-occupation-number-basis]] (with
$P_\pm^{(0)}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb C}$), and let $W(n,d)=\{\lambda\in\mathbb N^d:\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$
and $m_\lambda$ be the symmetric vectors of that theorem. Then:

(a) *fermionic configurations*: the map $J\mapsto\mathbf 1_J$ is a bijection
from the set of $n$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,d\}$ onto the set
$\{\lambda\in\{0,1\}^d:\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$; consequently
$$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\#\{\lambda\in\{0,1\}^d:\textstyle\sum_j\lambda_j=n\},\qquad \sum_{n=0}^{d}\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=2^{d};$$

(b) *bosonic configurations*: the assignment $\lambda\mapsto m_\lambda$ induces
a bijection from $W(n,d)$ onto the set of lines spanned by the orthogonal basis
$(m_\lambda)$, so the number of bosonic configurations of total occupation
exactly $n$ is $\binom{n+d-1}{n}=\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}$, and for every $N\ge0$ the
number of bosonic configurations of total occupation at most $N$ is
$$\sum_{n=0}^{N}\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\sum_{n=0}^{N}\binom{n+d-1}{d-1}=\binom{N+d}{d};$$

(c) *exclusion counts*: no fermionic configuration has an entry $\ge2$, so the
antisymmetric Slater index set contains no $\lambda$ with $\lambda_j\ge2$ for
some $j$; for $n>d$ there is no fermionic configuration at all and
$\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$, while for every $n$ and every $j$ the
bosonic configuration with $\lambda_j=n$ and all other entries $0$ occurs, so
no occupation bound holds in the symmetric sector;

(d) *consistency with the total occupation*: for every $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ one
has $\sum_j\lambda_j=n$, and for every fermionic configuration
$\lambda\in\{0,1\}^d\cap\{\sum_j\lambda_j=n\}$ likewise; in particular the
total occupation equals the particle number $n$ in both sectors.

**Slot convention.** For $\ell\ge1$, $S_\ell$ acts on $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}$ as in [[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. On one-based tuple positions use $\widehat{\pi}(k):=1+\pi(k-1)$ for $1\le k\le\ell$. The parameters of $U_\pi$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)$ remain canonical zero-based permutations.

(b) *Slater basis*: for every $J$ with $|J|=n$ one has
$e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{n!}\,P_-^{(n)}(e_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{j_n})$ and the
family $(e_J^\wedge)_{J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\},\ |J|=n}$ is an orthonormal family whose
closed linear span is $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$; it is therefore an
orthonormal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$,
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\binom dn$, and
$\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}=\{0\}$ when $n>d$. Moreover for every multi-index
$i$ one has $P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=0$ when two entries of $i$ coincide, and
$$P_-^{(n)}(e_i)=\operatorname{sgn}(\rho_i)\,\frac{e_J^\wedge}{\sqrt{n!}}$$
when the entries of $i$ are pairwise distinct with underlying set $J$ and
$\rho_i\in S_n$ is the unique permutation with $i_k=j_{\widehat{\rho_i}(k)}$;

(c) *symmetric basis*: for every $\lambda\in W(n,d)$ the vector $m_\lambda$ is
nonzero, the family $(m_\lambda)_{\lambda\in W(n,d)}$ is orthogonal,
$U_\pi m_\lambda=m_\lambda$ for every $\pi\in S_n$, and for every multi-index
$i$ there is a real number $\gamma_i>0$ with
$P_+^{(n)}(e_i)=\gamma_i\,m_{|i|}$; consequently
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ is the linear span of $(m_\lambda)$, the family
$(m_\lambda)$ is an orthogonal basis of $\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$, and
$\dim\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}=\binom{n+d-1}{n}$;

(d) *occupation operators*: for $j\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ the map
$$N_j:H^{\otimes n}\to H^{\otimes n},\qquad N_jx:=\sum_{i\in\{1,\dots,d\}^n}|i|_j\,\langle x,e_i\rangle\,e_i,$$
is a self-adjoint bounded endomorphism, the $N_j$ commute pairwise,
$\sum_{j=1}^dN_j=nI$, and
$$N_je_J^\wedge=\mathbf 1_J(j)\,e_J^\wedge,\qquad N_jm_\lambda=\lambda_j\,m_\lambda .$$
Consequently both sectors are invariant under every $N_j$, the joint
eigenspaces of $(N_1,\dots,N_d)$ inside $\operatorname{ran}P_-^{(n)}$ are the
lines $\mathbb Ce_J^\wedge$ (one for each $n$-element subset $J$, with
eigenvalue vector $\mathbf 1_J$), and the joint eigenspaces inside
$\operatorname{ran}P_+^{(n)}$ are the lines $\mathbb Cm_\lambda$ (one for each
$\lambda\in W(n,d)$, with eigenvalue vector $\lambda$).

Adopt the state and composition postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable and probability postulate in the reading of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] (P2), and the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4), and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ be the assigned energy observable of a declared isolated system with state space $H$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]), spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ and flow $U(t)=\exp(-itH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar)$ ([[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]]), and write $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$. Then:

(a) **Energy law and moments.** For every preparation $\rho$, every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ and every $t$,
$$\mu^{H_{\mathrm{op}}}_{\rho(t)}(B)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho(t)E_H(B)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho(0)E_H(B)\bigr)=\mu^{H_{\mathrm{op}}}_{\rho(0)}(B);$$
for the pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi$ likewise $\|E_H(B)U(t)\psi\|^{2}=\|E_H(B)\psi\|^{2}$. If $\psi(0)\ne0$ and $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, the mean and second moment of the energy law of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ are finite and time-independent. For any nonzero representative $\psi(0)$ their time-zero values are
$$\frac{\langle H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(0),\psi(0)\rangle}{\|\psi(0)\|^{2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\|H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(0)\|^{2}}{\|\psi(0)\|^{2}},$$
respectively. The displayed conservation of moments makes no assertion that these moments are finite for preparations outside this domain hypothesis.

(b) **Conserved sharp observables.** Let $(A,u_A)$ be a bounded assigned sharp observable that is compatible with the energy ([[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]] clause (f)). Then its outcome law is time-independent: for every preparation $\rho$, every Borel set $B$ and every $t$,
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho(t)}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho(0)}(B).$$

(c) **Stationary states are exactly the eigenrays.** Let $\psi\in H$, $\psi\ne0$. The pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary, that is $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, if and only if $\psi$ is an eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$: $\psi\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$ and $H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi=\lambda\psi$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. In that case $\psi(t)=e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\psi(0)$ for every $t$, and every assigned sharp observable has a time-independent outcome law in this preparation: $\mu^{A}_{[\psi(t)]}(B)=\mu^{A}_{[\psi(0)]}(B)$ for every $(A,u_A)$, every Borel $B$ and every $t$.

(d) **Status and exclusions.** No equilibration, relaxation, decay or convergence of the law of an arbitrary preparation is asserted; no moment beyond those finite at time zero is claimed; the converse of (b) — constancy of the law of a bounded observable in every preparation implying strong spectral compatibility with the energy — is not asserted for a general (possibly unbounded) $H_{\mathrm{op}}$; and the item is conditional on the isolated-system idealization of P4, asserting no apparatus realization and no empirical result.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition.

**(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b).

**(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$. If $A$ has no eigenvalues, every preparation has an atomless outcome law: each singleton has probability zero, while $\mathbb R$ remains the outcome space and the law is concentrated on $\sigma(A)$ as in clause (d). Zero singleton probability does not exclude real point values as realizations of this law; it supplies no normalized exact-value eigenstate. A finite-resolution record is read through its declared Borel bin, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2.

**(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

**(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation.

**(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be trace class ([[def-trace-class-operator]]). Then:

1. for every **nuclear representation** $Tx=\sum_j\langle x,u_j\rangle v_j$ of
   $T$ (operator-norm convergence of the partial sums,
   $\sum_j\|u_j\|\|v_j\|<+\infty$), the scalar series $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$
   converges absolutely and
   $$\Bigl|\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle\Bigr|\le\sum_j\|u_j\|\,\|v_j\| ;$$
2. the sum $\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$ depends only on $T$; denoting it
   $\operatorname{tr}(T)$, one has
   $$\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_j\langle v_j,u_j\rangle$$
   for **every** nuclear representation of $T$. This defines $\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   without assuming that $H$ has a Hilbert basis;
3. for every supplied Hilbert basis $E$ of $H$,
   $\operatorname{tr}_E(T)=\operatorname{tr}(T)$
   ([[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]]);
4. the trace is linear in the trace-class variable and bounded by the trace
   norm: for trace-class $S,T$ and scalars $a,b$,
   $\operatorname{tr}(aS+bT)=a\operatorname{tr}(S)+b\operatorname{tr}(T)$ and
   $|\operatorname{tr}(T)|\le\|T\|_1$.

derivations.claim: [The labelled operator on the product basis] By [F2] each $h^{(i)}$ is bounded and self-adjoint, so $H_{\mathrm{lab}}=\sum_ih^{(i)}$ is bounded and self-adjoint with $\|H_{\mathrm{lab}}\|\le N\|h\|$. On the product basis vector $e_i=e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_N}$ the $i$-th slot operator acts as $h$ on the factor $e_{i_k}$, giving $h^{(k)}e_i=\varepsilon_{i_k}e_i$; hence $H_{\mathrm{lab}}e_i=(\sum_k\varepsilon_{i_k})e_i$. Since every $U_\pi$ permutes the slots and $H_{\mathrm{lab}}$ is the sum over all slots, $U_\pi H_{\mathrm{lab}}U_\pi^*=H_{\mathrm{lab}}$. This proves (a).

[Sector eigenvectors] Let $J=\{j_1<\cdots<j_N\}$ and $i=(j_1,\dots,j_N)$. By [F3], $e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{N!}P_-^{(N)}e_i$; since $H_{\mathrm{lab}}$ commutes with $P_-^{(N)}$ by step 1.1 and [F3], $H_{\mathrm{lab}}e_J^\wedge=\sqrt{N!}P_-^{(N)}H_{\mathrm{lab}}e_i=(\sum_{j\in J}\varepsilon_j)\sqrt{N!}P_-^{(N)}e_i=\lambda_Je_J^\wedge$. Likewise, for $\lambda\in W(N,d)$ and any multi-index $c$ with $|c|=\lambda$ one has $P_+^{(N)}e_c=\gamma_cm_\lambda$ with $\gamma_c>0$ by [F3], so $H_{\mathrm{lab}}m_\lambda=(\sum_j\lambda_j\varepsilon_j)m_\lambda$; because the $e_J^\wedge$ and the $m_\lambda$ are orthogonal bases of the respective sectors by [F3], [F4], the spectrum of $H_N^\sigma$ is the finite set of the displayed eigenvalues with the configurations as multiplicities, and for $\sigma=-$, $N>d$ the sector is $\{0\}$. This proves (b).

[Partition sum and the zero sector] Normalize the symmetric vectors to $\widetilde m_\lambda:=m_\lambda/\|m_\lambda\|$; by [F3] these form an orthonormal eigenbasis, as do the Slater vectors in the fermionic sector. The trace is therefore $Z_N(\beta)=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal C_N^\sigma}e^{-\beta\lambda_\lambda}$, with the configuration counts $M_N^-=\binom dN$ and $M_N^+=\binom{N+d-1}{N}$ from [F4]. For $\sigma=-$, $N>d$, the index set is empty and the trace is the empty sum $0$. There is no eigenvector on $\{0\}$ and hence no ground eigenvalue, and its only operator has trace $0$, so no trace-one density or normalized Gibbs density exists there. In every other case [F4] gives a finite nonempty index set, so its finite sum of positive Boltzmann weights has $0<Z_N(\beta)<\infty$. For that case finite minima and maxima $E_0,E_{\max}$ exist, and for each configuration $e^{-\beta E_{\max}}\le e^{-\beta\lambda_\lambda}\le e^{-\beta E_0}$, because $\beta>0$; summing the $M_N^\sigma$ inequalities proves the two bounds. This argument allows negative configuration energies.

[Reading and stationarity] The pair $(H_N^\sigma,\mathrm J)$ is the model's assigned energy observable of clause (e) of the declared-model definition, so by [F5] its outcome law in a declared sector preparation $\rho$ is $\mu_\rho(B)=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{H_N^\sigma}(B))$; for the pure preparation of a sector basis vector $\Psi$ of step 2.1, $E(\{\lambda\})\Psi=\Psi$ and hence $\mu_\Psi$ is the point mass at $\lambda$. By [F5] and step 2.1 each such $\Psi$ is an eigenvector of the generator, so its pure preparation is stationary under the flow $U(t)=\exp(-itH_N^\sigma/\hbar)$ with $\Psi(t)=e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\Psi$, and the energy law of any preparation is the finite spectral law in the sector basis. This proves (d).

[Extreme energies and ground eigenspace] Work on a nonzero sector. For $\sigma=-$, each configuration selects $N$ distinct eigenvalues, so its energy is at least the sum of the $N$ smallest and at most the sum of the $N$ largest; these bounds are attained by the corresponding subsets. Thus $E_0=\sum_{k=1}^N\varepsilon_{(k)}$ and $E_{\max}=\sum_{k=d-N+1}^d\varepsilon_{(k)}$. A minimizing subset contains every mode with energy strictly below $\varepsilon_{(N)}$, contains no mode with energy strictly above $\varepsilon_{(N)}$, and fills its remaining places with modes at that boundary energy; this includes all choices allowed by degeneracy. For $\sigma=+$, the identity $\sum_j\lambda_j=N$ gives $N\varepsilon_{(1)}\le\sum_j\lambda_j\varepsilon_j\le N\varepsilon_{(d)}$; the two bounds are attained by putting all particles in a minimum-energy or maximum-energy mode respectively. Equality at the lower bound holds exactly when every occupied mode has energy $\varepsilon_{(1)}$. Finally expand a unit vector in the orthonormal sector basis of step 3.1: $\psi=\sum_\lambda c_\lambda b_\lambda$, $\sum_\lambda|c_\lambda|^2=1$. Then $\langle H_N^\sigma\psi,\psi\rangle-E_0=\sum_\lambda|c_\lambda|^2(\lambda_\lambda-E_0)\ge0$, with equality exactly when all coefficients at energies greater than $E_0$ vanish, that is, exactly on the ground eigenspace. Together with step 3.1 this proves (c).

[Conclusion and scope] Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (a) and (b), steps 3.1 and 4.1 prove (c) and step 3.2 proves (d). The argument used the finite-mode idealization, the declared non-interacting $h$ and the finite-dimensional spectral and tensor calculus; no interaction, spatial realization, infinite mode family, thermal state, equilibration or laboratory identification entered, which is (e).
